utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and just outside the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam registrar. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Madam Usher --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a couple of points, one very quick and then one of some substance. Your Honour, the first one is may I convert a contingent apology into an actual apology, Your Honour, because yesterday in relation to the maps if we had made a mistake and if there is confusion in relation to this map, then I heartily apologise. Your Honour, there were mistakes and there was confusion, therefore my apology is there on the table to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. And I should say that yesterday afternoon Mr. Krajisnik and I were able yesterday amicably to resolve that between us without any difficulty in a short time. So friends again this morning. On that, Your Honour, what -- I'm joking, of course. Your Honour, the point of -- of real substance is that we on our side, and I know the Prosecution have looked as well, Your Honour, because we do talk to each other, looked again at what had been said and Your Honours' ruling, a decision in relation to -- to the question of the use of the interview transcripts. And, Your Honour, I have to say that in the end we were unable to work out clearly where we were, and therefore, Your Honour, we are seeking guidance and we are depending on what Your Honours indicate, possibly an opportunity of making any necessary submissions. But, Your Honour, it is -- the Defence's understanding when we left court yesterday was that the interview transcripts were not in evidence except to the extent to which specific passages had been put to the witness which he had then confirmed, and to that degree one can then of course read those into his evidence. Your Honour, that was the position as we understood when we left court. When we had the opportunity for practical reasons, unfortunately rather late in the day yesterday, but the opportunity to look at yesterday's transcript, we began to be concerned that it really wasn't as clear as that and to wonder where exactly we were. We hope that is the position, Your Honour. If it isn't, then we are, with respect, going to have to look a little bit more at it. But may I simply ask the question first, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I answer that question, I will consult during the next break with my colleagues to see whether we have all the same answer to that question on our mind and then I'll give it to you on behalf of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we are ready. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom. I would like to take the time at this moment to assist you at -- to announce that for the contextual exhibits in relation to Zvornik and to Vogosca, we have not yet set a time limit for any objections. Mr. Stewart, if the Defence would like to raise any objections in respect of the contextual exhibits on Zvornik and Vogosca, it should be done within seven days from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you for that guidance, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I'd like to begin by turning to a couple of matters or a few matters that were raised yesterday. First of all, having looked at the transcript, it appears that we, because of a microphone problem -- we have an answer to a question that was not fully transcribed and then the question appearing later, perhaps it's helpful to simply make that clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I understand is that it was translated in B/C/S, but it was not translated in the first instance into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. If the Court is satisfied -- the Court knows the question to which I'm referring and we do have an answer on the record. So if that's satisfactory, I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, that question concerned receiving Legija of Arkan's group at the Crisis Staff. You also referred yesterday to the visit of Mr. Seselj to Brne's group in Ilidza two or three times. Is it when Seselj visited Brne's group, did you receive Mr. Seselj -- did you facilitate his meeting with representatives of the VRS and did Mr. Seselj visit soldiers and Brne's group with a representative of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to these questions and in relation to these questions, I fully stick to my original statement from 2003. The arrival of Mr. Seselj to Ilidza was not something that we had organised and we had not extended an invitation to him. He came on his own initiative. He visited the Brne's group. And on that occasion, I was not present. I was not at that venue, at Brne's venue. But I did receive Mr. Seselj in my office. We had certain talks, and I think we visited the Ilidza Brigade, but I also know for sure that we visited a part of the front line, I think of the 3rd Ilidza Battalion and the positions at an Energoinvest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday I also asked you whether the -- to whom or to which body the Crisis Staff, the Serbian Crisis Staff of Ilidza was subordinate to and your answer spoke generally of not a lot of hierarchy, of all coordination at the time was agreed with our leadership, et cetera. But I don't think the question of subordination, per se, was explicitly answered. Is it correct, Mr. Prstojevic, that the Serbian Crisis Staff of Ilidza was subordinated to the president of the Serbian assembly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff at Ilidza was basically set up and operated in line with the instructions that I saw here. And I've referred in the interview 093, I believe, 093. It is quite clear that the responsibility of the Crisis Staff had to do with the fact that they were accountable to the state and political bodies that issued those instructions and asked for them to be implemented. Basically, coordinating activities of the Crisis Staff would be subject to consultations and agreement with the top political and state leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, then two questions in response to that. First of all, let me turn your attention and the Court's attention to page 48 of the November 2003 interviews. And following some general discussion of the Assembly of the Serb people and the Crisis Staff, you were asked: "So did you understand that the Serbian assembly of Ilidza and the Serbian Crisis Staff of Ilidza was organisationally subordinated to the president of the assembly?" And you responded: "Absolutely, that's why it reported to it." Is that an accurate summation of the hierarchy or the -- between the Crisis Staff, the Serbian Crisis Staff in Ilidza and the president of the Serbian National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct and it can be seen on the basis of documents that we submitted to the president of the assembly straight after the setting up of the assembly. And it also transpires from the coordination that certain people from Ilidza were involved in together with the leadership from Pale. And we're talking about people such as Mr. Tomislav Sipovac, who was referred to here yesterday, as well as Mr. Ranko Mandic who amongst other things was in charge of the presentor -- and talks with the representatives of the European Economic Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday I also referred generally to a portion of your interview in which you provided an assessment to 99 per cent of the people you believed to be in the War Presidency at Pale and I failed both to cite the page on which that was contained and to make clear what your assessment was. So for the benefit of the record and the witness, the question at page 183 of the sequential transcript was: "And who were the persons who comprised the War Presidency of Pale?" And on page 184 the answer was: "There is that document that we looked, I think is the first one, document about mobilisation. I do not know exactly, but I suppose for 99.9 per cent, President Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, president of the assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the government, whether minister of defence or not, I do not know."

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely because we got no written document telling us who was in the War Presidency. We knew that on the basis of what we had been told, on the basis of our conversations and assumptions. So I can't tell with 100 per cent certainty that President Karadzic would have been there, although he should have been. So I stick to my previous assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I'd next like to move on to a new document, and that is an intercept dated -- I think the date that may appear on the list is 16 June, but I believe the correct date according to the document itself is 14. In any event it's 0401-3878.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Located at -- it's item 17, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Item 17.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P796.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Hello. Radomir. Yes I am. Is Obren there? Obren left to Bijelo Polje. He has a meeting there. Is he down there? [As read]. Yes. And who else is here from --. Dragan is here, Aco Kutlaca, too. I'll speak to Dragan for a bit. Okay. So, what's new, tell me. Well, nothing special. But they called me from Kasindol to tell me they did not get electricity. Is that right? They did not get it. There is no electricity. I don't know why. They did not. There are big problems there. Because -- I've just read it -- did he say [as read] anything about the water? I mean Dragan Despotovic -- he's somewhere. I mean this Dragan Despotovic. I see. Dragan is working on it. He will. Yes, him, I meant him. He's working on it. But it doesn't go so quickly. Yes. No, that part of work does not go easy. But they are for [as read] -- everything that simply -- Bogatici -- to provide the electricity for the Muslims, but they did not want to. It seems it is about Bogatici. Is something expected there? Yes, they will not do it from Bogatici. They will not -- from there -- Yes. They need to hide it somewhere. In the cellars and so on. Yes, okay. Would you like to speak to Dragan? Yes. Here you go. Hello? Dragan. How are you, Nedjo? Good afternoon. I'm fine. How are you? Well, it's not bad. How are you? Fine, but I have many worries, I can tell you. Sorry? I have many worries. What is it Nedjo? The things are not going well -- do you know about the latest news that the army was defeated? Shot at? Up there at Kasindolsko Polje. Yes, I do, Dobro Polje. Yes. They say that the shots were very precise. Well, there were no victims, but it could be said that they were rather accurate. Yes. But tell me, did they disconnect all the phones of the Turks in Kasindol? Sorry? Did they disconnect the phones of the Turks in Kasindol? All the phones are getting disconnected. They're getting disconnected? Everybody's. Had they been disconnected before? Theirs had been disconnected before. Yes, and -- Everybody's. And now the phones of our people are getting disconnected because there are indications to put to use telephones for them. That is the way those things are happening. But tell me this, please. Yes. What shall we do? Would it be good if we gave it a thought and if we organised people from outside to expel them all. Nobody needs to be shot or killed. Everyone expelled. That would be -- the might move. That would be [as read] -- let's say that you make preparations. I have a decision from before. Well, we tried it once but then there were some 'guardians' and it remained that way. Well, you cannot -- no they won't -- he will -- let him come make [as read] -- the people are still standing. When they arrive, they will go to hell. He will go with them, too. Agreed. Up to Bascarsija. Okay. Speak to Obren and -- When he comes. He went for a meeting. -- to consider so we can hear from each tomorrow to sort it out. -- to call you tonight or tomorrow morning, whenever you want. Fine, I will be absent. You will be absent? Okay. Then we'll send you the information tomorrow morning, Nedjo. I -- shall we hear from each other a bit earlier? The second issue. Yes. Do you have the Turks to load and unload the goods from. Yes, we have. Well, it doesn't seem to be right. People are complaining about it. I know. Why don't you sort it out? Well, that too should be sorted out tonight. Do something about that as well. Both things will be sorted out. Are they detainees? No, they're not. They're allegedly loyal. I don't know, something like that. They cannot find our people who would do it. This and that -- You can send the army. Okay. You task the army and if -- tie hands, compulsory work order, if you want, we can issue compulsory work order. Fine. Please, take both. Okay. Tell me, what are the chances for electricity? Not good, to tell you the truth. I would have to -- I will consider certain things tomorrow but it will be late for -- and for Vojkovici. It will be late? Yes, but I'll see -- General policy of water supply cuts is carried out in the whole town. That is only on the level -- to be. They don't give the electricity, we don't give the water. We'll try to do something about it, but -- Obren arrived. Would you like to speak to him, Nedjo? It's okay -- But I told you everything and you will speak to him. Do you have anything else? No. Say hello to Obren, and that's it, mainly. Okay. That is -- you do not have to share it with many people. Do it in a narrower circle -- We will sort out both things in a narrower circle. -- to consider and so on. No problem. How is Radomir? Is he helping? Well, I have no idea. Fine. Cheers. All the best. Cheers. Bye."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, who are you talking to in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular conversation, several issues were discussed, both civilian and security-related issues in the area of Kasindol --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic. Mr. Prstojevic, would you please carefully listen to the question. The question was not what subjects were discussed. The question was: Who was the person on the other side of the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person on the other end of the line was, as far as I can assume, Radomir Kezunovic who was one of the managers of one of the companies. The other person I was talking to was Dragan Ljubora [phoen] who was in charge of materiel, supplies, or rather the supplies of materiel and the supplies in general for the population that was present in the area. He was in charge of the logistic support.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to a portion of that conversation which is reflected on page 3 of both the B/C/S and the English translation. We see there that you raise the issue of what to do and "whether it would be good if we gave it a thought and if we organised people from outside to expel them all. Nobody needs to be shot or killed, everyone expelled." Who were the people from outside that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were referring to the people from the western side of Ilidza. Ilidza was divided into two parts. In the eastern part of Ilidza there were five local communes and the population there was 80 per cent -- 85 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. per cent Serb. My house is there in that area. The seat of the municipality and of the local authorities was in the western part of it, where most of the population lived and that was urban population mostly. These events were unfolding in the rural areas of Kasindol, which still today remains poorly populated and rural.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if I might leave Court for just five minutes. I need to telephone one of our team, something that is not easy to delegate. Might I do that? I shall not be far away. I'll be in the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but would you expect Mr. Tieger to continue, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honour. Yes, of course, and I -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it then that certainly Mr. -- I see Mr. Josse there --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse is here. He's not technically counsel, Your Honour, but I hope that would be satisfactory to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, this is exceptional, because usually counsel should be -- but at least one of counsel should be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's why I asked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under the present circumstances, I will allow you, knowing that you'll be well-informed after you return by Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's very kind, Your Honour. Thank you. I shan't not be very long anyway. And thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed to just add to my statement. I wish to mention the name of a person I omitted to mention which is Dragan Despotovic. He is an electrical engineer, and he was involved in solving the problem of the power supply in the area. And if I may continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, it might be more efficient if you permitted me to ask questions about the portions of the intercept that I'm interested in, then the other -- then the Court or the Defence can subsequently ask you questions about that rather than have you simply tell a narrative about the things you believe others may have an interest in. So you say that the people from outside were actually people within Ilidza, and so which people specifically did you want to consider organising to -- for the purpose of expelling them all?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A platoon of some 20 people from the Territorial Defence had to be organised, because the platoons were crossing over from the eastern to the western side to aid us when we came under attack. However, we were unprepared in this particular instance. We had not had men at the ready, and an investigation into this could reveal that this is true, the way I'm putting it here. What's more, a good many Muslims remained in this particular local commune throughout the war and still live there today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you're saying that in fact not all the Muslims from that local commune were expelled?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not because as you can glean from this we were under artillery attack from Muslim units, and that was the area of Kasindol, where my house was. So the discussion here had to do with this attack of theirs. When the attack came to a stop, the situation returned to normal and there are still Muslims today living in the -- in my neighbourhood, for instance, who had been living there during the war as well. And in the local commune where I live, there -- the Muslims there were not being expelled in any organised fashion. And that's exactly the local commune that is the object of discussion in this particular conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if they weren't being expelled in any organised fashion, then in what fashion were they being expelled?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims were not -- in Ilidza were not being expelled in an organised fashion and this can be proved for the entire -- for this entire area. It was in the areas that were -- combat activities were being conducted that Muslims were driven out. In 1992, there were numerous Muslim units in the area, and under such circumstances even thousands of households would actual move out, but both on the Muslim and Serb side. Throughout the war, many homes were left abandoned, those that were abutting the line of contact, the line of confrontation as the people were leaving the area. However, the Muslim and Croat population were allowed to go wherever they wanted to go if they wanted to. Initially, they were allowed to go wherever they wanted to go and then subsequently they were allowed to go to those municipalities where there were no combat activities under Croat control because the front line was held so strictly that civilians could cross these areas only through organised exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, after you raised the suggestion of organising people from outside to expel them all, Dragan mentions that: "We tried it once but then there were some guardians," and so apparently it didn't happen. Who were those guardians? Were they internationals, that is members of international organisations?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about these attempts. These were not international guardians because at this local area there were no representatives of the international community at the time. These were just our people who lived peacefully with their neighbours, and they were there to protect the people from those who were prone to aggressive outbursts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the proposed destination for these people, as in the intercept we listened to before the adjournment yesterday, was again Bascarsija. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Bascarsija is a commercial area known worldwide and there are no residential premises there. To this day Bascarsija symbolised the centre of Islam and it symbolises the Muslim part of the town. However, there are no residential premises there. There are just handicraft shops there and so on. Nobody -- none of those people who had been expelled ended up in Bascarsija to be put up or accommodated there because there was no accommodation for them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Further down on the page you refer to detainees. Where were the detainees or where did you understand the detainees to be held at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page is that concerning the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was the same page we were looking at before, page 3, towards the bottom. You have three-quarters of the way down the page: "Do you have the Turks to load and unload the goods from 'OKO'" it says here. And then there is some further exchange about that. And then you ask: "Are there detainees?"

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this area before the war, there was the prison there under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice, which continued operating into the war. There were convicts there who had been convicted for less serious offences like traffic violations. Now, in the war if there were any detainees or prisoners of war, they were put up in those prisons. Even before the war, it was usual for the prison to provide prisoners there for public works were whatever work obligation was required. And now I'm not certain for the latest stage how it was all regulated, whether this was under a work obligation or some sort of a different arrangement. From this conversation, we can see that there were Muslims who were unloading goods and that some of the citizens were complaining about this. And for this reason, I raise the matter for further discussion. Later on when the situation settled down, these people were hired on under a work obligation. 85 per cent of those who were under work obligation were actually Serbs, but for the rest these people were deemed to be loyal, not to cause any trouble, and this is the way it functioned until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So when you ask about detainees, was it your understanding that these were detainees at Kula prison or Kula and other places or other places? That's all I wanted to know, where you thought these people were.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from the Kula prison. They could only have been from the Kula prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Unless the Court has any questions, I'm moving on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would have one question, and that's the following. You said when you referred to Bascarsija, you are referring to the centre of Islam and that the Bascarsija, which I understand was a part of Sarajevo, was a place where you couldn't stay. So therefore, you could not have referred to that specific portion which was, as you said, a commercial area. At the same time, yesterday you explained that -- or at least it's part of the intercept, you said: "Take them, all of them to Bascarsija on foot," and you explained to us that you did not need to organise any transportation because it was so close by. So now, a simple question: When you said in that intercept we heard yesterday and when you said this same in the intercept we just heard, were you referring to some unknown place or were you referring to Bascarsija, a part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was always referring to one and the same Bascarsija. However, the civilians from the yesterday's intercept could not have been taken from the Kula prison to the line of engagement because what -- this was the idea and that's where the Muslims would take over because that was the extent of the territory that was under our control --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. You give a lot of explanations, but I have a very simply question. You said: I referred to the same Bascarsija in both the telephone conversations. Was that Bascarsija a part of the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do have one more question about this conversation, Mr. Prstojevic, before we move on. After you express and after you tell Dragan: "Would it be good if we organised people from outside to expel them," Dragan says: "That would be the right move." You say: "Well, let's say that you make preparations. I have a decision from before." What was that decision?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been a position that was taken as to how to deal with a situation where combat activities emerge, as they did in the area of Kasindol. But as I've said, following this particular conversation there were no -- there was no expelling of the population from Kasindol in any organised fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with the respect to the position on how to deal with the situation where combat activities emerge, was that your decision or a decision taken at higher levels and passed on to you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply, when combat activities emerged things took their course in a chaotic matter and then simply you had to take a decision on who could be present there or not. The decisions were not taken individually, but rather by collective bodies, in this particular case by the Crisis Staff. This was a very tumultuous period, one in which one had to take decisions instantaneously, because whatever had been discussed in the morning could prove to be inadequate or irrelevant for what was going on in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, could I again ask you to answer the questions rather than tell us a lot of things that are not a response to the question. In the telephone conversation you said: "I have a decision from before." You were asked what that decision was; you didn't answer that question. Then you were asked whether such a decision came from what level and there again there's no clear answer to that question. So again, now, the first question: The decision from before, what decision was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To put it simply, I don't know which decision is being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you just told us what the subject of the decision was, it was about the position. You said: "It could have been a position that was taken as to how to deal with the situation." That suggests that you know more about the decision, as you're telling us now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely why I was telling you this. The war situation dictated the moves to be taken. If this situation was critical in terms of the territory being in danger of being lost to the enemy, then very energetic steps had to be taken to save one's head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that decisions have to be taken in such a situation, but that's not a decision from before. A decision from before refers to a decision that had already been taken earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you mean and that's the way things should have been. But you have to understand what I'm saying. We had taken certain views and positions to enable us to -- to know how to react in a given situation because we would have failed entirely had we not known what to do when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... were those views you developed earlier, views and positions? What were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember precisely what they were. They were not in written form. It was as simple as this: Wherever they were combat activities, as was the case with Kasindol, very strict measures as far as possible, strict as far as possible were taken to secure the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that include expelling the population, including the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would mean that the population had to be moved out, if the entire area was under a threat or if it meant that the entire area would be lost to the enemy, or if it meant that the population would be in grave danger. This is precisely what happened in Kotorac which was mentioned in the yesterday's intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that if circumstances required you to do so, that you would remove the civilian population from the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but that meant that both the Serbian and Muslim populations were moved out, and this also meant that the -- and the Croats as well, and the population itself would move out on their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. I'd like to move on quickly to a couple of documents before we listen to the next intercept. The first is a document dated February 6th, 1993. It's a declaration of the agenda, the Ilidza SDS, and is found on the list at number 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This, Your Honour, would be Exhibit P797.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prstojevic, this document appears to be from some kind of official publication. Can you tell us how this was disseminated?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I'm thinking about the fact that documents which were not in the original and which don't bear my signature are not something that I should comment on. But I can comment on this document, even though I can't guarantee that this is a genuine document. Such a document - well, I'm not sure about the contents 100 per cent - was probably decided by the Municipal Board of Ilidza, probably February of 1993 in this specific form. It is divided into separate parts, and it has been circulated to the members of the Municipal Board, the local authorities, and then it was forwarded to the Presidency of the party and the main --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, looking at the translation of this document, is there missing a part of the translation in number 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps we should have that read out, Your Honour. You're looking at the -- the portion that appears immediately below the text. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems that the -- to be although not a signature, at least some reference to the author of this document and it does not appear in the translation, which might have some relevance, isn't it, from what I can read from the -- it seems that the name of the witness appears there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, do you see the document in front of you and the bottom of the -- if you look to the very end of the document.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the document and I can see it. I've told you what I think about photocopies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, would you please read what it says there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The president of SDS Ilidza, Nedjeljko Prstojevic, economist."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If a question is put to you, please try to answer that question, and there's no need to hear from you whether you consider that you could comment on something. You should answer all questions in accordance with the knowledge you have. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if you look, Mr. Prstojevic, at the section of the document that appears immediately following the heading "the tasks of Ilidza SDS in war according to the agenda," it says: "A black-winged vulture is looming over our Serb land from which we have lived immemorial. It is threatening to crush our Serb name, Serb culture, and Serb places of worship and to reduce Serbia to the Belgrade Pasavik [phoen]," and it also goes on to refer to taking arms in order to defend themselves from those "dishonourable and primitive Islamic jihad and Ustasha enemy." First of all, Mr. Prstojevic, is that language that appears in this document familiar to you from documents produced by you in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this kind of language. It's a language calling for fight and strengthening the morale of the Serb nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me quickly show you one additional document. That's a document dated May 10th, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, it occurs to me that when Mr. Tieger referred a moment ago to language appearing in this document familiar to you from the document produced by you in 1992, that it might be convenient for the future to have that identified specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm doing that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought it was a different document we were coming to. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I did say "additional." That was probably confusing --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's ET0227-9812, item number 8.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P798.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you would hang on to both documents for just a moment. Mr. Prstojevic, would have a look at Exhibit 798 that was just presented to you. Now, that is a document which bears your signature, is that correct, and I presume, therefore, was produced by you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never drafted a single document single-handedly. It was a whole team that would be drafting it and then the Municipal Board would approve it as a declaration on the work under war conditions, and there were quite a few members of that board, or else it would be up to the Crisis Staff. So the same goes for this document, appeal for the Serb officer who thinks of his homeland. It was approved by the Crisis Staff, and I was a signatory, as I was the first man of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we look at the first two paragraph of that document, that is of P798, it appears to contain essentially the same language found in P797 that we discussed earlier. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Of course if the people drafting it are the same and if they're doing it at more or less the same time, of course they would be using this romantic language which would be calling for people to go and fight and sacrifice themselves, because quite a few people were killed in Ilidza in excess of 900 and 3.001 were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking back quickly at P797, it also refers in a couple of places to the tasks and goals of the Ilidza SDS including, in the third paragraph of the agenda, the task of victory over the enemy and the liberation of Serb land. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the reference to that is, but it is possible Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that there is one and this is something that had to be said, should have been said at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking at the portion of the document under the declaration of the agenda of the Ilidza SDS, that's the portion at the beginning of the -- 797. In the third paragraph it begins -- well, the third indented paragraph it begins: "On 4 April, 1992, the Serb people of Ilidza led by the SDS rose up to defend their centuries' long ancestral homes," and it continues about the formation of strong TO units and the MUP and the liberating and strengthening control over all Serb territories and giving significant help to Serbs on territories of other municipalities. Anything about that paragraph with which you disagree?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we move on to the next intercept then. That's ET02279812. It's a conversation between Mr. Prstojevic and Mr. Mandic and is dated the 2nd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P799.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- 799A would then be the transcript and 799A.1 would be the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- excuse me, that's item 15 I believe. Yes, 15 on the list. I apologise. I confused the registrar by providing an erroneous ERN. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I believe this is -- in fact, it is a document that I believe you've had a chance to review before. So perhaps in light of the technical difficulties in playing the intercept, we can distribute the transcript, both to the witness and to the Court and the parties, and proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be provided with the transcript, B/C/S pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, since normally we have an opportunity to listen to the transcript, I want to give you an opportunity to look at that transcript. So take a moment to look it over and let me know when you've reviewed it again sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And is it also correct you had an opportunity to listen to that intercept in your -- during the course of your interviews and recognise the voices of those of your own and Mr. Momcilo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer you to page 3 of the transcript, that's both in the B/C/S and the English translation. Mr. Mandic indicates to you that it has come to -- he says: "Our attention and that of the government that you are issuing ultimatums to some Turks, evicting people from certain settlements and people respond badly to it, they are abusing this, those Muslims and the media, and so on." Did you understand during that conversation that Mr. Mandic was calling you to tell you that he and others were concerned about the bad publicity that was resulting from evicting people from certain settlements?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand it that way. Quite the contrary, I denied it to the minister straight away; I said it wasn't true. I took it as an introduction to tell me that employ this judge who came along later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you've referred to the judge, you're referring to Fadil Musanovic who Mr. Mandic mentioning on page 4 of the intercept transcript?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Mandic wants to have Mr. Musanovic take a position of some sort so that "we," he says here, "will be able to say that we employ Muslims, Croats, and Serbs." And he asks you then to place two or three Muslims somewhere. So you understood that Mr. Mandic was calling because he wanted Mr. Musanovic to be put in a position so that it could be publicised. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I understood it, and the rest is just conjecture on the part of Mr. Mandic. He obviously had a great deal of time to tell stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandic seemed to understand, although you denied it, as you say, that you were evicting people from certain settlements. And then he expressed concern about the publicity that was bringing. That part's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't think Mr. Mandic was concerned about this one bit, because quite simply it did not apply to Ilidza. Because not a single operation except for Kotorac, which was initiated by the JNA, actually took place there in the form of an offensive prior to that conversation. We were simply defending ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you think Mr. Mandic -- or you say that Mr. Mandic was wrong in saying to you that you were evicting people from certain settlements?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him, you've seen it. I told him -- I mean, I was just a mayor. I was of a lower rank and I nevertheless contradicted the minister twice in this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what you actually say to Mr. Mandic after he expresses concern that evicting people from certain settlements is very bad publicity for us. You then tell him: "We didn't say it, not in public." And then again you say: "Well, we didn't say it in public, nor did we write it." So you're assuring Mr. Mandic, are you not, that there shouldn't be any bad publicity because there's nothing public about it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says in my translation, and I'm sure that that's what it said, I said: "Please." Where did I ever say such a thing. I don't know, but we never said that publicly anywhere; this is not our policy. And that makes it quite clear that evictions were not part of our policy, and I even have documents which prove that I allowed the non-Serb population to stay at Ilidza in order to protect them, and they held out until 1995, the very people that I issued those papers to and then they had to leave anyway. And somewhat clumsily I said, there is no document or proof or war propaganda or press or anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. You assured Mr. Mandic that there's no proof to that effect. Now, after Mr. Mandic tells you what information has come to his attention and that of the government, he asks you: "Please, do not do anything like that. Consult with Djeric first and those people up there because this is bad publicity." So did you understand Mr. Mandic to be saying, before you do something like this, talk to us first because there's an issue of the publicity it generates?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously that's the way I understood it, but this entire conversation is just propaganda for a man who has nothing better to do, and he's simply criticising something that both he himself and his people were involved in and he was trying to get me dragged into it and criticise me whilst I was simply fighting for survival at Ilidza. And -- I mean, he was in the free territory on another location. He was an idle man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, he was at Kula, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it had been liberated from the point of view of the centre of Ilidza, where we had been totally surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact, wasn't he at Kula from the very beginning of the war and there ...

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was at Kula for the most part since the beginning of the war. He was located at a position where all of the events concerning Kotorac and the interview took place. He did not have to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, I would like you to take a look at page number 2, and more specifically your -- the second term that you speak on page number 2. And in English, [In English] "not in public, that is not our policy."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's page number 4 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I'm very sorry. You're right. Have you found this passage, sir? Page number 4, the second time that you speak, and then the third time that you speak on this page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is what you're saying -- [In English] "We did not say that, not in public" -- "we did not say that, not in public." [Interpretation] So it seems that what you are saying is that you said it but not in public, and in fact in the next sentence this is what you say -- [In English] "We did not say that in public." [Interpretation] So it seems that what you're telling us is that you did say that in private but you didn't say that in public. And in fact, you didn't write it. I think that during this telephone conversation the reply that you're giving is ambiguous, so I would like to get some further explanation about this. You could have said: I've never said that. But you said: "I did not say that, not in public."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could refer back to the same page but a different section where Mr. Mandic tells me: "Ah-ha, I have two questions for you." And I say: "Yes." I was saying: "Yes, yes," because I was listening. That meant that I was listening and that I understood what he was telling me. And there you have me saying "yes" again, because this meant I've understood -- yes, I've understood. And this is something that you can see recurring in my conversations. That's why I say here: "Yes," but where did I say this? The key point is that this was not our policy, and I still claim so today. With the exception of Kotorac, we did not have a policy of expelling civilians in any of the areas except where the circumstances required the population to leave the area because of the combat activities or where the population wanted to leave on their own initiative. As for the part where I say that we did not say it in public, had this been written or said in public, this would have been disseminated by the media and it would have disturbed the general public. In actual fact, we did not say such a thing, write such a thing, or have anything of the sort as our policy. In the conversations I had with Mr. Mandic and some other conversations, I noticed that we were -- they were discussing things that had nothing to do with reality. Sometimes he seems to be saying things as if he's trying to make a joke or pull someone's leg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please point at where you flatly deny that evictions took place in this telephone conversation. Where did you say, "Such evictions never occurred or happened"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the very same page, after this one long intervention where I say: "Well, yes," but please tell me wherever did I say this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say that in response to a remark made by Mr. Mandic, who said the following: "What did you say? You are not responsible for their safety or something like that." And then you respond: "Well, yes, but where did I say this?" So you there, according to a logical interpretation, but please come up with something else, if there is, you are denying that you said that you're not responsible for their safety or something like that. It's not - looking at the core of the conversation - a denial of any conversation occurring. If you'd like to comment on that, you'll have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, in my conversation with the minister, I focussed on him saying that we had issued an ultimatum to the Muslims in a settlement, that they were to move out within 24 hours. And that's what I was focussed on, and I was denying that. Secondly, as for the issue of the safety for the Muslims in Ilidza, the situation at the time was so difficult. There were cases of murders committed against Serbs by Serbs, or the Serbs themselves opening fire on a part of the municipality that was inhabited by the Serbs. Whenever you try to protect someone, you're exposed to fire. And I wasn't omnipotent there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll have a break, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we've spent quite some time on the interpretation of telephone conversation with Mr. Prstojevic. If the language of a telephone conversation is clear and if questions put to the witness result in explanations of which the Chamber has difficulties to link those explanation to the language used, it's not necessary to go on forever and seek such explanations for the whole of the conversation. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber hopes that it has understood well your question for clarification as far as the position of the transcript of interviews is concerned. I take it that if from the answer of the Chamber you would feel that we have not properly understood your question, we'll hear from you. The transcripts of the interviews, that is the November 2003 and the recent interviews, are not tendered nor admitted into evidence. That means that to the extent that the witness is confronted with it by reading parts of it, that's of course part of the record now and to that extent it's part of the evidence and of course the responses of the witness. But the transcript, as such, are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- that's very helpful indeed. We're extremely grateful for that on the Defence side. The only residual issue there would be for complete clarification when Your Honour says that when the witness is confronted by reading parts of the transcript, that's of course part of the record now. Well, of course that's clear. And Your Honour says "and to that extent it's part of the evidence and of course the responses of the witness." Your Honour, we would suggest one further step is needed for that to happen, that that can only be -- it's part of the record; of course, it can only become part of the evidence if the witness does say here in court, Yes, I confirm that, yes, I adopt that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're now triggering is a different matter, and that is if there's any inconsistency between what the witness said in his interview -- and again, if it's not on the record, it's certainly not in evidence. The Chamber will have to consider whether -- if a witness says, This is what the -- this is what the transcript of the interview says, but I deny that that's the truth, then of course we are confronted with a question which is not an easy one, whether it would be exclusively the answer given during his testimony, which is inconsistent with the transcript of the interview, whether that would exclusively be in evidence. I noticed that where there's any inconsistency between -- well, let me call it "prior inconsistent statements," that in the common-law world, as far as I understand, the answer to whether the testimony would be the final word or not is answered in different ways from what I understand under English law, more strictly saying that evidence is only the testimony given in court, whereas under US law there seems to be circumstances under which a Chamber might also take into consideration what a witness said during an interview. We'll have to check whether any such inconsistencies, substantive inconsistencies do appear in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. We do with English law, what was the law last week is not necessarily the law this week at the moment. It's some weeks since I've been to England, so they haven't kept me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say they are now more flexible in England in using the transcripts of previous inconsistent statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I would say this whole area is in a state of flux, Your Honour, that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took a position which might not be unfavourable for the Defence as far as English law is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's understood. With respect, I would endorse that as -- with respect to the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having reminded us, we'll check what happened over the last couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just say this -- try to clarify my own mind rather than anything else, Your Honour. Of course, when a passage is put to the witness and it's on the record, of course, it is also in a sense, it is -- if you like, it's in evidence before the Tribunal that he did previously say that, so conceptually that's -- and then we move on to these next questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we see whether there is any substantive inconsistency as far as the content is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. I can leave it there for any -- for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it as a matter of fact that it would not be in dispute since there are audio recordings that -- well, this is what the witness -- of course, apart from mistakes in the transcripts, et cetera, but I didn't hear any dispute as to whether the witness was interviewed and whether these transcripts reflect the -- what he said during these interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, it appears they did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is not the time and place for an extended discussion. I would simply note that I -- based on my understanding of the state of the law and the modern trend, there the Court is in a position to resolve any such inconsistency in favour of either the previous statement or the testimony given. And the modern trend in both the US and in Britain as I understand it is to dispense with that distinction and instead permit the Court to make its best judgement on the basis of all the information available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, to be quite honest, I knew that this was the position on US law but I did not follow up all the modern trends in English law. And apart from, I've not even talked about Canadian, Australian, whatever is there. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, in the intercept we just listened to, Mr. Mandic urges you to consult with "Djeric first and those people up there." Yesterday you told the Court of the hierarchy of the Bosnian Serb leadership in 1992 from the top down. You explained it was Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Prime Minister Djeric, and so on down the line. Was Mr. -- so with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik at the top, was Dr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik the highest authority in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a difficult question to answer. I did say that Mr. Krajisnik was the most important person to ask, given that Mr. Karadzic was very busy and that Mr. Krajisnik was in many aspects much closer to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you seem to be explaining that now as a function of who's busy and who's not, but let me refer you then to what you said in one of your interviews, the interview conducted in May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, has the matter not been dealt with yesterday or am I wrong? I'm just trying to find it. I'm just trying to find what was said about -- well, at least the witness said that they were more oriented to Mr. Krajisnik as far as -- in terms of cooperation for the area of Sarajevo. He clearly said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, something very close to what has just been said in evidence appears then at the top of the very next page, 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You asked, Mr. Tieger: "And between President Karadzic and President Krajisnik, did on -- one or the other have more influence or authority over the Sarajevo region? And if so can you tell Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. us why." And then the answer was: "If we take everything into account for the region of Sarajevo, Mr. Krajisnik was more important to us because we thought of him as one." So there clearly in response to a question of who was more authoritative in the Sarajevo area, the witness has expressed some preference for Mr. Krajisnik rather than Mr. Karadzic. So I wonder what this would add.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to make sure that all the factors are elicited, Your Honour, and the extent of that authority is made clear, as the witness has done on a previous occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you do not spend too much time on it, you may confront him -- you took him to what page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That would be page -- it was the May inter view, the May 2005 interview, the second set, and it's on page 17 of that second set. And Mr. Prstojevic had been saying -- had been talking about military operations and said: "In he sense it was the decision of the top leadership that during the offensive or defensive operations every single potential is used for the assistance of the army or MUP." And then he was asked: "When you say 'the top leadership,' who are you referring to?"

utterances.speaker: MR. PRSTOJEVIC SAID
utterances.text: "I always mean two people, which is President Karadzic and President Krajisnik. Having said that, President Krajisnik has more influence and authority over the Sarajevo region because he is a man from here and he controlled political policy in the area of Srpska Sarajevo because he is just -- he is a person from here."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although there might not be much new in it, what has just been read to you, Mr. Prstojevic, is that consistent and what you wanted to say when you gave your testimony yesterday about the position of Mr. Krajisnik in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it's consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we next look at item number 0297-064 -- 0064. And I believe that's a document dated 20 September, 1993, and it's item number 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, that's in evidence, Nielsen, tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although the P number from Nielsen isn't there, but the Chamber understands where to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prstojevic, the document dated September 20th, 1993, is a document issued by the Republika Srpska Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Serbian public security station in Ilidza. And before I turn you to a particular portion of that document, I'd like to ask you a question first, and that is: Apart from the issue of expulsions that we have -- we discussed earlier in your testimony, were there other measures taken against Muslims in Ilidza to get them to leave?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not expel any Muslims in an organised fashion from Ilidza, and we did not undertake anything else against the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that repressive measures were taken against Muslims which resulted in them increasingly fleeing from the territory?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if any repressive measures have been taken, but whoever was in a minority in a given area would not have been safe. And the population moved en masse. No matter what population, if they were not in a majority, they would tend to move to those areas where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, then, if I can to the second -- the last paragraph of page 2 of the English translation. I'm trying to find it for you in the B/C/S. That paragraph begins: "All detained Muslims," and it's on page 3 of your translation, again the second-to-last paragraph. It states that: "All detained Muslims were thoroughly interrogated in order to extract useful information regarding their intentions. Repressive measures undertaken against them for various reasons resulted in them increasingly fleeing and moving out of this territory." Does that refresh your recollection about repressive measures taken, and can you tell us, if so, what those measures were?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Srpska, and this is the first time I've seen it. And it seems to be harking back to the past quite considerably. This is a passage based on the previous two passages on the first -- on the same page, and it refers to past activities prior to the 1st of April, 1992, or at the very least, at some point in the beginning of April. And I'm not aware of any repression of any sort, whether MUP might have done something that we were not aware of. But basically, organise the repressive measures just did not exist. As to whether anyone took it upon themselves to do something, I mean paramilitary units at a later stage, but here we're talking about a period of time before the war broke out; that's my understanding. So this is prior to the 4th of April. You can see that on the basis of para 4. This was before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're not suggesting that things got better for the Muslims in Ilidza after the war began, are you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really, but it is not really clear to me what it says, that there were expulsions of Muslims in that period and there were not. I mean, chief of police in Ilidza at that time was Edin Mlivic and he was there in Ilidza until, roughly speaking, the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the document also clearly refers to the activities that followed the creation of the Serbian police station, as you'll note from an earlier paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you two very simple questions, Mr. Prstojevic. First, in one of the telephone conversations we heard, you are informed that -- where you are asked: "But tell me, did they disconnect all the phones of the Turks in Kasindol," I take it you were referring to Muslim inhabitants of Kasindol. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's correct. The question was asked, but I was the first person whose phone was disconnected at Kasindol for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, when I want to know when your telephone was disconnected, I will ask you. Isn't it true in this telephone conversation you were informed about the fact that the telephones of the Muslims in Kasindol were disconnected before? And do you consider this to be a -- an oppressive measure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's correct that the phones were being disconnected, but I really don't think it's a repressive measure because starting from the 19th of June the entire area of Ilidza was disconnected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the Muslims were first disconnected and that only for reasons given in this telephone conversation, only later the whole of the telephone connections were disconnected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's correct, but it was for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The one doesn't exclude the other. Are you aware you're speaking of the telephone conversations about exchange of -- you were even thinking in terms of 5.000 Muslims to Serbs. Were these 5.000 people waiting voluntarily until you had made up your mind to exchange them or were they kept in a situation where they would not be free to move anymore but they had to wait for any exchange arrangement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did mention this symbolic number because in the central part of Ilidza that was the approximate number of Muslims living there. But it was a fact that Muslims did want -- not allow Serbs from the other side to come out and we did allow them to go where they wished to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's then the meaning of exchange, whether it would be 5.000, 3.000, 2.000? You said they were free, so there was no exchange because the Muslims are free to go wherever they wanted. Isn't that your testimony? And, Mr. Prstojevic, perhaps I should inform you that this Chamber has heard evidence before on matters in relation to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm pleased to hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm just telling you that we heard evidence. I'm not going to give it to you. My question was whether exchange would not imply that people were not free to go wherever they wanted, but they had to wait until someone had arranged for an exchange. So they're not free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On our side, they were free to go when they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How could you then exchange them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used this term by way of comparison. If people wanted this, we would do what we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answers are not well understandable for this Chamber, Mr. Prstojevic. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, let's next take a look at some remarks you made in July of 1992, which can be found reflected in the record of the 17th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's previously in evidence, Your Honour, and we'll be distributing the relevant pages of that transcript. It's P65 of the Treanor documents, tab 182, binder 13. It's also P529, the Hanson materials, tab 392, binder 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, the document in front of you is a record of the 17th Bosnian Serb assembly session held, to the best of my recollection, on the 24th or the 26th of July, 1992. The record reflects that you attended and that indeed you spoke and addressed the assembly, saying in part, and I'll begin at the beginning: "Mr. President, honourable MPs, I have decided to say a few words and ask a few questions and I'm being asked by the citizens of Sarajevo. Namely, when the Serbs started the uprising in Sarajevo and when they seized control over certain territories, there was no government, or at least it was not known where it was then. Moreover, we even did not know if Mr. Karadzic was alive during the first couple of days. When we learned that he was alive and when he visited us in Ilidza and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory and even extended their territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been majority." Now, first of all, Mr. Prstojevic, can you tell us about the visit following the starting of the uprising in Sarajevo by the Serbs during which you and the others in Ilidza were encouraged?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said a few things about that, namely on the 17th of April I think the Crisis Staff at Ilidza held a somewhat shorter meeting of the government of the Serb people of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it was attended by Presidents Krajisnik and Karadzic. At any rate, the session itself was very encouraging for us and I can only say one sentence that I remember very well that was uttered at that session. Dr. Karadzic said that no citizen of Ilidza should be harmed in any way, and to a certain extent he criticised us. But our defence lines were not safe enough and then they said, Yeah, you have these defence lines which are not safe and you want the government to be based to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in part, at that meeting there was a discussion about the security situation, the military situation in Ilidza. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the staff commander of the Territorial Defence, Dragan Markovic, reported on the security situation in our area and on the basis of that the president got the impression that we were unsafe and that Ilidza could fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there also a discussion about where the seat or the headquarters of the political authorities would be?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means because we wanted the seat to be in Ilidza or perhaps another part of Serb Sarajevo which was under our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik tell you at that meeting where the seat of the political authorities would be, or did they tell you they would let you know later?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said precisely that they would be telling us about that at a later stage, and that's how the meeting ended. But if I may, at that stage I would like to point out that there is an inconsistency here in the translation. It says "chased away" or "expelled Muslims," whereas I said "pushed back," which is a different thing all together. So instead of "expelled" it should be "pushed back."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a translation issue or a transcript issue? Could you please verify that, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you identify the portion of the transcript you're looking at that contains the passage or the words you just spoke about?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please identify that portion where you say that it does not reflect properly your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the tenth line on the first page, and "in some parts extended their territory and pushed them back from the territory where they had the majority." It's not "expelled" but "pushed back," and it is about the local community where an attack was launched against us, but the Serbs and Croats were in the majority there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pushing back, what's that different from expelling? Could you explain to us how you push someone back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To say "expel" is a rather nasty way of chasing away non-fighting population. Pushing back, on the other hand, as in this case where the Muslims first launched the armed activities, combat activities, at Rakovica and we lost a part of our territory and then we engaged in this combat, we pushed them back. We then took over the entire local area and placed it under our control --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that to say that finally only combatants were not present anymore or did the civilian population stay in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the majority of the civilian population left with the combatants, and the rest of them left afterwards gradually because that was the free territory, Kiseljak, where people could walk freely at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could they not walk freely where they were at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, yes, because it was a Croat municipality, Kiseljak, which was not engaged in war against Ilidza, and the Croats and Muslims were not at war amongst themselves at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now -- but they -- from the place where they were pushed back, were they not free to move in that area where, as you said, they were pushed back from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had an immediate link to the Muslim territory because it is in the direction of Central Bosnia. It is not an urban area; it is a peripheral part. It is a rural area with about a thousand to 1.140 inhabitants. So I gave a list investigators from the pre-war municipality of Ilidza according to each and every local community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you're not answering my question. My question was whether from the area where you said they formed a majority and from where they were pushed back, were they free in their movements in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what you mean. Do you mean in the area which was under our control or Muslim control which was bordering our territory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the area where you said you pushed them back from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
