utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was where the front line was to be set up. The ones that remained within Serb territory -- were free, to move freely. And if they had gone over to the Muslim territory, they would have had even greater freedom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Mr. Prstojevic, that your reference to the territories where Muslims had actually been in the majority was a reference to Kotorac and Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I meant was Ratkovica only and Kotorac, apart from that one part, that one-third that had always been kept under Muslim control. I mean that part remained Muslim throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, during your interview in November of 2003, there was a discussion about this speech at the National Assembly. And you were asked at page 80 which territories you were referring to when you were talking about the majority of Muslims in particular areas. And you said: "At that time that could only be referred to Kotorac and parts of Stup 2. Nothing else." Then you were asked: "Could it refer to other places such as parts of Dobrinja or possibly north of the Ahatovici." And your answer was: "Sorry, I forgot here about Dobrinja." Does that refresh your recollection, Mr. Prstojevic, about the territories to which you're referring in your remarks at the 17th Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is true. Dobrinja has about 48.000 inhabitants. This speech at the assembly took place after the operations at Dobrinja and we had control over about 2.000 homes there, nothing more than that, which, roughly speaking, would mean 8.000 inhabitants. So this can't be a correct answer, and Dobrinja could not have been meant there even though I was not prepared to properly answer that question. So that's what I must have said. Also, Kasindol that we've been talking about, a good part of that area remained under Muslim control throughout the war, perhaps 40 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say "2.000 homes" under your control, meaning 8.000 inhabitants, those are homes in which Muslims had previously lived and in -- and which were now available for Serbian refugees. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say it's incorrect. We're talking about homes, accommodation units. This is an urban part of Dobrinja where Serbs and Muslims lived together and there were about 24 Croats in all in all of Sarajevo. So that makes it easy for you to calculate how many of them could have been in that particular urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The 2.000 homes that you were mentioning in your earlier answer were homes in which people no longer lived and were now available for other people to live in. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not houses, family houses. These were apartment buildings. And since they were in the -- along the line of engagement, we were not able to accommodate anyone there throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I don't want to dwell on this point longer than we need to, but those were homes -- those were homes or apartments or flats or housing units in which people had previously lived and which they were no longer living which now became available. And those are the 2.000 homes you're referring to, right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but flats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask a question. I refer to the document which -- last document you've shown us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this same page, on this same page. Mr. Prstojevic, you say -- [In English] "Ilidza and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory and even extended the territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been majority." [Interpretation] So if I have properly understood, there is a question about the translation on a sentence. I would like you to read the next sentence, Witness. You say -- [In English] "Brought the government of Sarajevo to the Serbs in Sarajevo, namely we -- namely we," one word illegible, "that we had to slow down our war operations because we were virtually deserted by the ex-JNA. The JNA did not give us the materiel or the approval for certain operations." [Interpretation] So what was this approval for certain operations? [In English] -- "or they did not give you the approval for certain operations?" [Interpretation] Therefore, the military of the JNA did not approve you, did not give you the approval you needed for certain Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. operations. What do you mean by that? In fact, you seem to be complaining about something. You seem to regret something. You wonder and ponder what the politicians, leaders in Sarajevo, Serbs in Sarajevo, have done and you are complaining for the fact that you have not received certain approvals for certain operations. I would like your comments on this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basically, we were quite disorganised in the Sarajevo area. We were surprised by the war. And then when, thanks to the lucky circumstances, we managed to retain a large part of our territory. On the 4th and 5th of April, the people and the units asked that we should have control also over the areas where the Muslims and Croats were in the majority. Even at that point in time, on several occasions a cease-fire was agreed upon and this was brought about by Mr. Koljevic, among others. The cease-fire would be arranged, for instance, because of the evacuation of barracks and for that purpose not a single gun shot was to be fired in Ilidza. And we had to honour that. The second point is that we were not happy with the JNA; quite the contrary. The Muslims in Ilidza were initially better armed than we were. For this reason, we were lagging behind in equipment, and that's -- it was by pure chance that we managed that maintain control over the area, but this of course had its toll where you would have a dozen TO members killed and 50 others wounded in a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to insist on -- I would like to have a comment on the words of the approval of certain operations. [In English] "JNA did not give us the materiel or the approval for certain operations." [Interpretation] So what is it about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This meant that at that time we were faced by requests to seize control over some parts of the area which was pretty easy, did not require and did not cause many victims. However, we enjoyed no support whatsoever from the JNA. What's more, we were even told to hold back our operations and were required to observe such requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And which were the reasons for this advice which was given to you? According to you, what were the reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part, JNA staff included people who simply sought a secure position and a satisfactory remuneration. Some of them were pro-communist and believed that Yugoslavia was going to survive one way or the other. There was the movement for the preservation of Yugoslavia. And they must have accorded the same treatment to the Muslims and the Serbs. In the morning, they would give some weaponry to the Serbs, in the afternoon to the Muslims. And this would be done by one and the same commander, for instance. At the same time, they would give advice to either side to stay put in terms of any operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I proceed just for the record, I wasn't clear on whether the witness was reading that portion or paraphrasing that portion of the transcript. The booth, I'm told, has a copy of the B/C/S transcript, and if they do I'd just like to have them read the sentence that begins at line 6, after the opening remarks, line 6 of the first full photograph beginning [B/C/S spoken], and ends at line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the booth has the text of these minutes and the tape-recording of the 17th session, and I am referring to ERN page number 0214-9561. If it could be slowly read and translated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "When we found out that he was alive and when he came down to Ilidza among us and gave us some encouragement, the Serbs in Sarajevo who were in the area maintained -- retained certain territories under their control and even expanded control over the territory in some parts and chased the Muslims away from the territories where they were practically a majority."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's different, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's different in quite a few material respects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I could not follow what the witness said before, whether he actually read or paraphrased that portion of the -- that portion of the minutes of this meeting. Could I ask the interpreters whether there could be any confusion as to the terminology in translating the original B/C/S where we earlier heard "pushing back" and where we now hear "chasing away," whereas on paper we have "driving out."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honours, that the closest translation of the term "potjerali" in B/C/S is "to chase away."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, you followed the explanation by the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was double-checking with my case manager as well, and, yes, I do see that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This having been clarified. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, when you were speaking about that portion of your remarks earlier, you provided the Chamber with a word that was not reflected in the transcript but that -- and that suggested a kind of military operation. I don't want to repeat the correct translation to you -- the correct translation of the word that appears in the transcript to you because it will -- it may -- let me do that because you'll get that word back clearly. The word that appears in the transcript is "chasing away." Now, why did you substitute a different word with a different connotation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the translation I have here I can read the word "potjerali," but I would never use this term because it's not germane to the context because potjerali means something else. The last time I thought I saw the word "potisnuli," [phoen] which is the adequate term to be used, given the context at the time. I wish to inform the Trial Chamber that I did not receive the translations of the interviews that I had; therefore, I have no idea what I said in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in 2003, Mr. Prstojevic, if we look at pages 73 and 74, you also challenged the word that actually appears in the transcript, only on that occasion you said that what you had actually said was not "pushing" but "inspiring" those Muslims away. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but this confirms that my position remains the same today, compared to what it was then because that's what this event was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So in your view, is inspiring the word you used or the right characterisation of what happened?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. By defeating the Muslim army, the territory was freed from the Muslims who were in the area. The fact is that prior to this period there were combat operations in Dobrinja and in the airport settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I comment. I'm having discussions here about the linguistic aspects. It does get terribly confused, Your Honour, because it appears that what is happening -- when the witness a few minutes ago said, "well, it wasn't this word, it was that word," that's because the witness is now getting then the B/C/S translation of a word used by Your Honour in Your Honour's English question. He's now getting back a B/C/S translation of English words and we don't know for sure whether those B/C/S words are matching what he originally said in the interview, which was translated into English and is now being translated back again. It's absolute linguistic chaos, Your Honour, if I may use that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I invited you at a certain moment to identify the portion where you said it did not reflect properly your words. You then said: "It's the tenth line on the first page," and then you said: "And in some parts extended their territory," and then you went on. When you gave this answer, were you reading what the minutes say or were you replacing what you considered to be an incorrect reflection of your words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was reading the part in the minutes where it says "potjerali," to chase away, it doesn't say "protjerali," to expel. Obviously it doesn't read here, and that's what the linguists would know. And I'm telling you these things because I know what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, I checked in the original and where there seems to be a difference between "potjerali" and "protjerali," where the witness said he read that part as "potjerali", it seems that the version without the "r" after the "p" is the one that appears in the original. But the matter has been sufficiently clarified at this moment. Whichever party would further like to consult the audiotapes and what the witness read is free to do so and to address the Chamber in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would wish to hear the audiotape, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that one of the words used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, the parties were invited to check the audiotape of this hearing, if they would have any need to do so. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour I'd like to turn next to document ET02237180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's number what in your list, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Item 24, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 24. Madam Registrar, that would be number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P800.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, Exhibit 800 is a document that bears the heading of the Republika Srpska, Ilidza war commission, and you are indicated as the signatory of the document, the issuer of the document. This document is a decision following a session of the war commission on April 2nd, 1993, considering the problem of the return of Croats and Muslims and the decision is that the return of Muslims and Croats to the territory of Ilidza Serb municipality is forbidden. First of all, Mr. Prstojevic, on a number of occasions you've told us how much the Muslims of Ilidza wanted to leave and how much they didn't want to come back. If that's the case, why was it necessary to issue a decision to forbid them to come back?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you that I cannot comment on the documents that are photocopies rather than originals because I do not consider them reliable. But I have already commented on this so I will do so again. I believe the document was issued at the time when the Muslims and Croats started fighting each other. As a result, from the area of Kiseljak which was 12 kilometres into the free territory, there were no combat activities there, the population started entering the area without any control from either the Muslims or the Croats, and the Croats in Kiseljak were not happy with the situation. We were on good terms with them. At the same time, it posed a security threat for us and we were hardly able to guarantee safety for ourselves, let alone for anybody else. The document states that the necessary conditions had not been met. The document, however, allows for certain exceptions according to an established procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to avoid whatever confusion, Mr. Prstojevic, was this decision taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, myself, do not remember the decision; however, having read the text I believe it was indeed taken under those circumstances. But it simply states that a Muslim was going to be safer in Ilidza than in Kiseljak. But this was definitely at the time when the Muslims and Croats were fighting each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've some difficulties in seeing that this document states that Muslims were safer in Ilidza than they were in Kiseljak, in fact it says that they were permitted to return to Ilidza, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct; however, they were fleeing the area towards us. Over 30.000 Serbs had crossed our territory at the time and there were also Croats and Croatian units that were fleeing from Central Bosnia. And this passage of the Croats across our territory was going to be regulated at the higher level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The decision simply says that: "Muslims and Croats are forbidden to return," and return means that they once were there and they could not come back, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This applied to that specific period because the necessary safety precautions had not been taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you say it's limited to a certain period, when was this prohibition lifted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that decision at all, but I know that even today sometimes people can't go back to some places because it's not safe for them to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break. Mr. Stewart, you're ready to start to cross-examine the witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd first like to ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, would you have any idea of how much time you would need for cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is pretty difficult, Your Honour, but I -- I realise Your Honour realises it's difficult. The best estimate I could give now would be something like about three hours, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- Your Honour, that really is only that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking for --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, it's a friendly inquiry. I take it that way, Your Honour, and my friendly answer, Your Honour, is that the best answer is the best I can do is -- is three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it could guide you. The Chamber has interfered with the examination-in-chief on a more frequent basis than usually done, although Mr. Tieger might disagree that we did not have the same frequency before. And I take it, Mr. Stewart, that you are well in a position to assess what kinds of questions the Chamber has put to the witness which may already indicate that part of his testimony needed to be further explored and that the Chamber is aware that there was a need. At the same time, if you are aware that the Chamber is aware that further exploration is sometimes further needed, this could help you understand what's still necessary in cross-examination and what might not be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I always try to read the entrails, and I will continue to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 11.00 -- to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please -- Mr. Tieger, is there anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just very quickly, Your Honour, I don't want to either dwell on this issue or expand it unduly, but if this is a helpful intervention at all then it seemed to me the time to do it was now. I had an opportunity to speak with the booth. I know at the end of the discussion the Court drew a distinction between "potjerali," which is "chase away" or "drive away," and "protjerali," "expel." The word originally used by the witness when he was discussing the remarks was "potjisili," "push back."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, when he read, when he had drawn our attention to line 10, et cetera, and then he used a different word from the word that appears in the minutes, the written minutes of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and that word was "potjisili," "push back."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this is on the record. If Mr. Stewart would disagree, then we'll certainly hear from him but let's not ... Pushing back and expelling does not necessarily contradict each either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We just haven't covered that in the B/C/S classes yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you'll be cross-examined by Mr. Stewart, counsel for the Defence. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, we notice --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't suggest, Your Honour, it's likely to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We notice you take a notebook when you come to give evidence. Our observation, Mr. Prstojevic, if you would confirm this, is what you do when you're asked a question you jot down just a little note to make sure that you got the question and you got a reminder of the question. Is that right? Is that what you're doing?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was never told I shouldn't be doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're not being -- well, I'm not in charge here, Mr. Prstojevic. I'm not through anybody suggesting that. At the moment I'm just trying to get it clear. So that is what you're doing. May I just ask to confirm then that you're not at any point -- you're not turning back to consult any other notes, apart from just what you jotted down about the particular question you've been asked. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I on the Defence side have absolutely no objection to that process, which we can easily observe from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You do not object, Mr. Tieger does not object, the Chamber does not object, so let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, in your interview, and this is at page 6 of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Unless otherwise stated, Your Honour, I'm always referring to the continuous 207-page big chunk of transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the transcript your interview at page 6 you say that you were the secretary for inspection in the municipality of Ilidza from 28th June, 1991, "at multi-party elections I became the head of the Serb Democratic Party of Ilidza." Did you mean to say multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Multi-party elections took place in 1992. And on the 28th of June, 1991, we had our own regular intra-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, that's exactly my point. You -- there were multi-party elections we know in November 1990. When you referred in your interview to multi-party elections you said from 28 June, 1991, "at multi-party elections I became the head of Serb Democratic Party," you actually meant the SDS internal elections, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then at page 43 you said that you had -- you said you'd been involved in the party and you'd been there - clearly the SDS - some 25 days before the elections in 1990. So sometime around the beginning of June, is that right? You actually joined the SDS, did you? I beg your pardon. I'm sorry, misread that. I retract that. I'm causing confusion. You became involved in the party some 25 days before the elections in 1990. So is this right you became a member of the SDS in early November 1990 just before the multi-party elections. Is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I signed the papers joining the SDS on St. Peter's Day in 1990 at Skenderija. But because I was busy with some private family matters and affairs and my work at the company, all that was basically brought down to those 25 days before the elections because at certain meetings at the place where I used to live in Kasindol such requests have been made and so we got down to business.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you say in a nutshell what brought you to join the SDS at that point?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a highly educated man and somebody who used to go on business trips to Austria at the time a great deal, I was able to discern that a slightly vague scenario was developing as far as the fate of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina were concerned. It is quite clear that the Party of Democratic Action was likely to win the elections, that amongst the Croat population, the Croat community, HDZ would win. And Serbs seemed to be distributed amongst a number of parties, SDP, the former communists, the Socialist Alliance of the Working People, where I was offered the post of president. And then last but not least, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason I'm doing this, may I say, is because in the interviews, frankly, there is a lot of confusion about Mr. Prstojevic's precise political history and positions, which I hope to clear up with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, first of all it's correct, isn't it, that at those multi-party elections in November 1990 you were elected as a deputy to the Sarajevo City Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Then at the -- as we have heard at the -- in the June 1991 SDS elections, you became the president of the SDS in Ilidza. And in your interview at page 43 you said: "I just by accident became the president of the party." Now, I'm not asking for some enormous elaboration, Mr. Prstojevic, but when you say you "by accident became the president of the party," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that means that by accident I was the president of the party and the mayor at the same time. At those inter-party elections I did not want to stand as a candidate for the Municipal Board of the SDS party. But on the occasion of the assembly which took place on the 28th of June, 1991, and there were about 250 members of the assembly at that time, requests were made for many candidates for come forward and therefore the candidate who won the most votes would become president and the second in line would be his deputy. And so, almost against my will, I won most votes at the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said in your interview you -- it was by accident you became the president of the party. Now, can I just get this clear. You became the president of the Ilidza SDS on or about the 28th of June, 1991. That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when did you become the president of the Municipal Assembly of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became the president of the Municipal Assembly on the 5th of April, 1992. War was already underway and for about seven to ten days I was being persuaded by other people to actually accept that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So just looking at page 11 - you haven't got it in front of you, Mr. Prstojevic - just to clear this up. At the foot of page 11 of your interview, Mr. Mitford-Burgess -- it just says, Mr. Prstojevic: "You told us previously that on the 28th of June, 1991, you were voted into position of president of Municipal Assembly of Ilidza." And your answer was: "Municipal Board of the SDS of Ilidza or president of the political party." So do we understand that you were correcting Mr. Mitford-Burgess at that point, you're saying, no, you've got it wrong, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, I wasn't elected president of the Municipal Assembly at that point. I was -- I became president of the SDS which is the same of being the president of the Municipal Board of the SDS? Is that all correct as I've just put it to you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then from the 5th of April, you were the president of the -- as you've said the president of the Municipal Assembly. That was not, was it, a professional, paid position at any time? Is that correct, it was unpaid?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You refer to something different. You refer to being the secretary, and the passage in question is at page 9 of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITFORD-BURGESS SAYS CORRECTLY
utterances.text: "The position that Mr. Prstojevic obtained was the president of the Municipal Board of the SDS party, Ilidza," and that's put as a question. You say: "Yes." Then Mr. Tate Haris with the OTP says: "Did that consume most of your time up until the outbreak of war?" You said: "No." I said: "Okay, what else were you occupied doing?" And you said: "As the secretary I was obliged to work at least eight hours evermore." Now, is that the position which you describe as the secretary for inspections?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. According to my contract with the Sarajevo railways company, on the 1st of February 1991 I was appointed as secretary for inspections. Basically, I wanted to become secretary for economic affairs, but somewhere in the course of that process somebody else was asked to take that position and it was felt that I could do a good job as a secretary for inspections. And this is what I did all the way until the 5th of April, considering that there was a lot of construction work going on in Ilidza without planning commissions. And there were quite a few problems at that secretariat. And there were quite a few parties and we had to do a great deal of work. And I even did not manage to use up all my annual leave for that day -- for that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, to get it clear then, that position that you are talking about as secretary for inspections, that was part of your -- your paid employment, your normal, paid employment?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So at page 16 of the interview when Mr. Mitford-Burgess says to you, you said, "Okay. Going back to the Municipal Board at Ilidza there was a local civilian -- was there a local civilian government or local combined government of all three parties or all parties?" And you said: "Yes." And I take -- we take it, please confirm, that the three parties being talked about are the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. My paid employment was as an inspector. And at Ilidza after the multi-party elections we had an agreement with the HDZ and SDA and we set up a joint coalition government. And on the basis of how many each votes got, we distributed portfolios. And I must say that we had fairly harmonious relations amongst the leadership of all those three parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess immediately after that continued: "Did you play a role in that civilian government?" And your answer was: "I was a secretary for inspections, or a secretary for inspections," but Mr. Prstojevic, please confirm if this is correct that from what you said your position as secretary of -- for inspection works was actually not a role in the civilian government but was part of your job.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The job of secretary for inspections would have been within the government. So I was one of the members of the Executive Board of the municipality of Ilidza. Because we had this coalition government and the Serbs, that is to say the Serb Democratic Party, was given the portfolio for inspections. Muslims got, for example, the defence affairs. And the secretary of the government, that post went to Croats, and so on and so forth. And the Muslims got to appoint the president of the Municipal Assembly, the Serbs got to appoint the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, and the Croats got to appoint somebody as an expert within that secretariat, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Prstojevic, in summary, is it this, that although the position of secretary for inspection works became part of your paid employment from day-to-day, that the decision on that appointment was essentially local political decision?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed, or rather elected to that position on the basis of an assembly decision, a decision of the assembly of Ilidza, which included the representatives of all parliamentary parties elected in the month of November 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Radomir Kezunovic, he was -- was he your predecessor as the president of the Ilidza Assembly before you took that role in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was the first president.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And at page 17, I don't know whether you can help with this, Mr. Prstojevic, but at page 17 of the interview, Mr. Mitford-Burgess put it to you: "And the only role you played in this municipal government was as the secretary for inspection works." And you answered that question by saying: "The organisation of local government in the municipalities looked this way." And then you set it out in some detail which I won't go into. And Mr. Mitford-Burgess then said: "And this is an organisational chart of the municipal, the local parliament, local civilian parliament, Ilidza." Was that organisational chart, can you remember now, prepared by you or prepared by Mr. Mitford-Burgess and his colleagues?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see an organisation chart here in the Serb language, but I believe that there is no reason whatsoever for Mr. Mitford-Burgess to write anything I did not say. I can, even now as civil servant from 1990, 1992 give you the organisation chart for the municipality of Ilidza and the government. And of course it should tally with what you have here. I might make a mistake, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I'm not going to invite you to go over that ground again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just ask if that organisational chart, which one would suspect it might be in the OTP files, might I overnight have a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would it be available for Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If it's available to me, it's available to Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's music to my ears [Realtime transcript read in error "years"], Your Honour. That's all I can ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- now, Ilidza, we can see this from the map. Ilidza is a municipality. It appears to be roughly 20 kilometres across east to west and about 10 kilometres north to south. Does that sound about right to you, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's approximately right but our front lines in the war went further than that. We were surrounded from both sides, and especially to the west in the urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. But moving on then, Mr. Prstojevic, in your interview at page 19 you gave some figures for the population or inhabitants of Ilidza. And the figures you gave were 29.000 Muslims, 25.000 Serbs, 10.000-plus Croats, and you said you couldn't remember but Yugoslavs were bigger or more than Croats, over 10.000 Yugoslavs, and there were some others. In your -- just pausing there but for a moment then, please. In the evidence that you gave yesterday, the figures you gave were 25.000 Muslims, 22.000 Serbs, 10.000 Croats, 8.000 Yugoslavs. The difference is -- between those figures is -- are relatively obvious. Is the -- is the position this, Mr. Prstojevic, that it follows from that that you are only in a position to give a very rough estimate of those figures?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, if I gave you this information yesterday, I must have made a mistake because I must have felt that I did not have to be all that specific as to the number of inhabitants. However, when I spoke to the investigators I gave them a list from Ilidza and there is a proper breakdown of population per each local community. And you can tell clearly how many inhabitants were in what community. But these figures, 25.000 Muslims, 25.000 Serbs, and 10.000 Croats, and about 10 or 8.000 Yugoslavs are probably more accurate. But there is the original document which gives you a proper breakdown and all the specific information and I really don't think it is necessary for me to try and pinpoint it exactly because I might even make a mistake. And you do have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prstojevic, in fact I'm not going to press you that it's necessary, but as His Honour indicated earlier, please, if you would answer the questions and leave the assessments of what's necessary or useful to others, that would be appreciated. The -- you gave a list to the interviewers; that was a list prepared by you, was it? I'm talking of a list of the population numbers.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a document from 1991 which indicates the official statistical data, the census, and the breakdown of the local community and I think it's a good-quality document. And I wonder if any other municipality in the area of the city of Sarajevo had such a detailed record. It is an official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we can wonder about that, Mr. Prstojevic. But do we understand that it wasn't actually prepared by you, but it was got from some other source, that you handed a copy over to the interviewers in November 2003?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only gave a copy of the document, which originates from the office of statistics for the town of Sarajevo. That's where the census was processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make the same request. If that document is available to Mr. Tieger, might it be also available to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that whatever's available to Mr. Tieger's in this respect available to you Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said before it was music to your ears, it's translated and I'd like to correct that for the record that it's "music for your years," but I would not allow that to remain on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, if I daughter had been in court, she would have made a comment about that. But, yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Prstojevic, you talked about Mr. Krajisnik, and this is at page 22, you were asked about Mr. Krajisnik's attendance at a Municipal Board meeting or meetings in Ilidza and you said this is at the foot of page 22: "Mr. Krajisnik" -- well, I'll lead into it. It -- the question from Mr. Mitford-Burgess was -- I'm going to start a little bit early up. Mr. -- both Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Velibor Ostojic participated sometimes on occasional basis in the work of the Municipal Board. Mr. Krajisnik for special reasons and special cases and Mr. Velibor Ostojic because he was from Ilidza, even for the territorial reasons, he was often more present" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Am I going too fast, Your Honour? I thank you for the reminder. "Mr. Krajisnik, for special reasons and special cases and Mr. Velibor Ostojic because he was from Ilidza, even for the territorial reasons he was more often present because someone" -- well, I'll skip the next sentence and then it says, Mr. Mitford: "You're saying that Mr. Velibor Ostojic and/or Mr. Krajisnik from time to time attended the SDS assemblies at Ilidza and gave directions or instructions to the SDS members." And you said: "They took part in participation, in the work of the assembly."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: "Yes." You: "Mr. Krajisnik in particular was present at one meeting of the Municipal Board, maybe two months after my election." Now, Mr. Mitford-Burgess had put it to you that you were saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but I think the record is going to be confused if I don't address this now. It appears that Mr. Stewart began by reading Mr. Prstojevic's remarks, but inadvertently indicating that that was a question by Mr. Mitford-Burgess. As I see the transcript, Mr. Mitford-Burgess asks: "Did you as the president of the SDS Party of Ilidza receive instructions from these people?" And then Mr. Prstojevic goes on to make the comments that are reflected in the first part of the transcript from which Mr. Stewart just read beginning with: "Both Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Velibor Ostojic participated sometimes."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is absolutely right. I see that Your Honour. I had noticed at the last second that it would make more sense to start higher up. But I hadn't made that clear. Thank you. The -- those were -- the document in front of him can see, but for the record, of course, I acknowledge that. The -- so then it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was you, just to get it absolutely clear, it was you, Mr. Prstojevic, saying: "Mr. Krajisnik in particular was present at one meeting of the Municipal Board." But Mr. Prstojevic, can you confirm, Mr. Krajisnik never attended assembly meetings in Ilidza, did he?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of which assembly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let's go back then. Mr. Mitford-Burgess said -- I'll ignore, with all respect to Mr. Ostojic now. Mr. Mitford-Burgess says in his question: "You are saying that Mr. Krajisnik from time to time attended the SDS assemblies at Ilidza." So my first question is: Was there such a thing as a meeting of the SDS Assembly in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were SDS assembly sessions in Ilidza like the one on the 28th of July, 1991, at which I was elected president. Of the high-ranking political leadership, Mr. Velibor Ostojic and Mr. Jovo Jovanovic, president of the SDS city board were present at the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, now first of all just a small point. You said there were SDS assembly sessions in Ilidza like the one on the 28th of July, 1991." You meant June 1991, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But you are talking then about -- not about any organ of Ilidza but assemblies of the whole SDS party that happened to be held in Ilidza. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You caused confusion when you said he asked whether he attended the assembly sessions because there are of course the Ilidza assembly sessions as well. There are also party assembly sessions like those of the SDA, HDZ, and SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I'd -- I'm trying to clear up confusion at the moment, but I'm not sensitive about what you said. The -- there was such a -- an organ or a body as the Ilidza SDS assembly, was there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Yesterday when I was indicating the organisational hierarchy of the party, I omitted saying that on lower levels there were SDS assemblies at the city level, at the local level. And as a rule, these were electoral bodies electing officials and discussing on an annual basis the activities taken by the organs on their level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. But quite separately from the Ilidza SDS Assembly, we've got what I'd call for want of a better phrase perhaps the national SDS party assemblies, one of which was held in Ilidza on the 28th of June, 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of June, 1991, at Ilidza, the assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party for Ilidza was in session; therefore, of the local assembly of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik didn't attend that meeting, did he?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik did not attend that particular meeting, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it correct that Mr. Krajisnik never attended any meeting of the SDS Ilidza assembly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but during my term of office he did not attend any of the sessions of the Ilidza SDS Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But you did say in your interview at page 22 that he was present at one meeting of the Municipal Board. And to clarify, you were meaning he attended one meeting of the SDS Ilidza Municipal Board, were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- sorry, if Mr. Stewart is indeed trying to clarify confusion. The -- there are two -- there are a number of references to attendance at the Municipal Board. It begins with the comment that -- of attendance on an occasional basis -- or "sometimes on an occasional basis and the work of the Municipal Board ..." "Mr. Krajisnik for special reasons and special cases ..." Then the phrase -- the portion of the transcript in -- which Mr. Stewart is referring says in particular present at one meeting, and I suppose the question then is whether "in particular" refers to that meeting or -- or to Mr. Krajisnik in particular, but focussing unduly on that one portion without having it in context, I think, is not completely fair opportunity for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it as a matter of fact that Mr. Stewart is aware that if he focuses on one portion only that in re-examination you would create the context. And at the same time, Mr. Stewart will certainly be aware that it makes not much sense to forget about the context if that context will at a later stage be restored anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, I must say that was one of Mr. Tieger's most unhelpful interventions. What I'm doing here is I'm clearing up confusion which is plainly created by the questioning in the interview where the tangle of which body is what appears throughout this document and that's what I'm doing. I'm focussing on it because that is the only way a clear picture will emerge and it will emerge more quickly if it's not confused by going go back up the page to the questions we've already covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My question, for clarification, please, Mr. Prstojevic, when you talked in your interview, you said: "Mr. Krajisnik in particular was present" -- I'm not asking you about the meeting at the moment, Mr. Prstojevic -- "was present at one meeting of the Municipal Board," you were talking, were you, please confirm, about the SDS Ilidza Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a meeting of the SDS Municipal Board in Ilidza just about at the time I indicated here --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I said expressly, that I was not asking you about the meeting. I just wanted an answer to the question about the identity of the board, and you have answered that, and I'm coming with the next question. So that was the body which you said Mr. Krajisnik was present at one meeting and you said that he attended for special reasons. And you went on in an answer at page 23 of your interview to say -- you were asked to describe by Mr. Margetts, so I I'm not going to ask you the same question again, he said: "Please describe to me the special reasons for Mr. Krajisnik's attendance." And you said, simply: "The members were requesting presence of someone from the high levels, some official, for they were requesting persons present. They were requesting presence of some officials or they were requesting to organise some speech or something in the municipality in the local community." So, Mr. Prstojevic, is this right that that one attendance by Mr. Krajisnik at the SDS Ilidza board was in the nature of a -- you wanted a political celebrity or you wanted someone to come along on that occasion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to explain. What I said here was true. On many previous occasions, other functionaries were present, including Mr. Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic, but always on our insistence. In such circumstances, whoever was available at the time was free would come and we would be grateful for them assisting us in our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that looks like a spot on time and point on which to conclude for today, if that suits Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Prstojevic, we'll finish for the day -- could you please keep your earphones on. We'll finish for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom. And I again instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you're still about to give. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 17th day of June, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
